title: Measuring the weather: thermometers, rain gauges and wind vanes

summary.text: Hang a thermometer in the sun and it can read many degrees more than one in the shade, in the same air. A thermometer shows how warm the thermometer itself is, and sunlight heats it. So weather stations keep their thermometers in the shade, inside a white box with slatted sides. A rain gauge measures rain as a depth in millimetres. A wide pot and a narrow jar with straight sides catch the same depth of rain. A wind vane turns to point to where the wind is coming from. Write these readings down every day in a weather diary, and patterns appear: the warmest time of day, the wettest week, the usual wind.
summary.art: A city balcony with a thermometer hanging under a small white paper roof, a plastic jar with a ruler on the ledge, and a card-and-straw wind vane on a bottle, with a child writing in a notebook.

intro.hook: The radio says it is 34 degrees in Chennai today. The thermometer on Nila's sunny balcony says 45. Both thermometers work. So which one is telling the truth about the air?
intro.text: Weather is what the air is doing right now: how warm it is, whether rain is falling, and which way the wind blows. To compare one day with another, or one town with another, people measure it. In this unit you measure temperature with a thermometer, rain with a rain gauge and wind with a wind vane. You find out why a thermometer must be kept in the shade. Then you keep your own weather diary, like the weather scientists of India.
intro.art: Two thermometers side by side on a balcony grill, one in bright sun showing 45 and one in shade showing 34, with a small radio on the table inside.

outcomes: I can measure the temperature of the air with a thermometer, and explain why it must be kept in the shade.
I can run a fair test that compares a thermometer in the sun, in the shade and under a white paper roof, and say what my results show.
I can measure rain in millimetres with a straight-sided rain gauge, and explain why its width does not change the depth.
I can make a wind vane, and use it to say where the wind is coming from.
I can keep a weather diary for a week and find a pattern in it, such as the warmest time of day.
I can tell how people in Korea in 1441 found a better way to measure rain, and why digging into wet soil gave the wrong answer.
I can read a weather report: the highest and lowest temperature, the rain in millimetres and the wind.

terms.meaning: What the air is doing at one place and time: how warm it is, whether it rains, how windy and how cloudy it is.
terms.example: This morning in Kochi the weather was warm, cloudy and still. By evening it was raining.
terms.art: One window shown three times in a day: sunny morning, cloudy noon, rainy evening.

terms.meaning: How hot or cold something is. We measure it in degrees Celsius.
terms.example: On a summer afternoon in Hyderabad, the air temperature can be 40 degrees Celsius.
terms.art: A thermometer beside a glass of ice water and a cup of hot tea.

terms.meaning: A tool that measures temperature. The red liquid in a glass thermometer takes up more space as it warms, so it climbs the tube.
terms.example: A weather thermometer hangs in the shade, so it measures the air.
terms.art: A glass thermometer with red liquid and a scale marked in degrees.

terms.meaning: The unit for temperature. It is written °C. Water freezes at 0 °C and boils at about 100 °C.
terms.example: A comfortable room is about 25 °C. Your body is about 37 °C.
terms.art: A thermometer scale with 0, 25, 37 and 100 marked, beside ice, a fan, a child and a kettle.

terms.meaning: The temperature of the air, measured with the thermometer kept out of the sunlight. This is the temperature in a weather report.
terms.example: The weather report says 36 °C. That was measured in the shade at a weather station.
terms.art: A thermometer in the shadow of a white box, with sunlight falling all around it.

terms.meaning: A white box with slatted sides that holds thermometers. It keeps sunlight off them but lets the air flow through. It is also called a Stevenson screen.
terms.example: Weather stations all over India keep their thermometers in a weather screen on legs, above the grass.
terms.art: A white wooden box with slatted sides standing on four legs on a patch of grass.

terms.meaning: A container that collects rain so that we can measure how much fell.
terms.example: A straight-sided plastic jar with a ruler beside it is a simple rain gauge.
terms.art: A clear jar on a balcony ledge with a ruler taped to its side and a little water inside.

terms.meaning: A small unit of length, written mm. Ten millimetres make one centimetre. Rain is measured in millimetres.
terms.example: After a heavy shower, the water in the rain gauge was 12 mm deep.
terms.art: A ruler, close up, with the tiny millimetre marks between 0 and 1 cm picked out in red.

terms.meaning: How much rain fell, measured as the depth of water it would make on flat ground if none soaked in or ran away.
terms.example: Chennai gets most of its rainfall between October and December.
terms.art: Rain falling on a flat steel tray, with a ruler showing the depth of water on it.

terms.example: The wind makes the clothes on the line flap and the coconut leaves sway.
terms.art: Clothes flapping on a balcony line, with leaves blowing past.

terms.meaning: The direction the wind is coming from. A wind that comes from the west is called a west wind.
terms.example: The southwest monsoon is named for where it comes from: the southwest, over the Arabian Sea.
terms.art: A map of India with a big arrow coming in from the southwest across the sea.

terms.meaning: A tool that turns in the wind, so that its arrow points to where the wind is coming from.
terms.example: A wind vane on a rooftop points west when a west wind blows.
terms.art: A metal arrow on a pole on a rooftop, with letters N, E, S and W below it.

terms.meaning: A tool that measures how fast the wind blows. Most have three or four cups that spin faster when the wind is stronger.
terms.example: An anemometer on an airport tower tells pilots how strong the wind is.
terms.art: Three small cups on arms spinning on top of a pole.

terms.meaning: A notebook where you write the weather at the same times every day.
terms.example: In her weather diary, Kavya writes the temperature at 8 in the morning and 3 in the afternoon.
terms.art: An open notebook with a table of dates, temperatures, rain and little drawings of the sky.

terms.meaning: A place where weather is measured with standard tools, in a standard way, at set times.
terms.example: The weather station at Chennai airport, in Meenambakkam, measures the temperature, rain and wind every day.
terms.art: A fenced patch of grass with a white weather screen, a rain gauge and a tall pole with a wind vane and cups.

terms.meaning: A scientist who studies the weather.
terms.example: Anna Mani, a meteorologist from Kerala, helped India make its own weather instruments.
terms.art: A woman scientist in a sari checking a rain gauge at a weather station.

terms.meaning: The highest and the lowest temperature of the air in one day. They are often called the max and the min.
terms.example: Today in Madurai the maximum was 37 °C, in the afternoon. The minimum was 26 °C, just before sunrise.
terms.art: A newspaper weather box showing Max 37 and Min 26 next to a little sun and moon.

explanations.concept: What we measure when we measure weather
explanations.definition: Weather is the state of the air at one place and time. The main things people measure are temperature, rain, wind direction, wind speed and cloud.
explanations.description: Words like 'hot' or 'very rainy' mean different things to different people. A child from Shimla and a child from Chennai would not agree on what 'cold' means. Numbers let everyone compare. Each measurement needs its own tool. A thermometer measures temperature. A rain gauge measures rain. A wind vane shows wind direction, and an anemometer measures wind speed. Clouds are still mostly judged by eye, by how much of the sky they cover.
examples: 'Very hot' in Delhi in May might be 45 °C. 'Very hot' in Bengaluru might be 36 °C.
A weather report gives the maximum and minimum temperature, the rainfall in millimetres, and the wind.
explanations.art: Four tools in a row: a thermometer, a rain gauge, a wind vane and a cup anemometer, each with a label.
explanations.context: This card says what weather is, and which tools measure which part of it.

explanations.concept: A thermometer shows its own temperature
explanations.definition: A thermometer can only show how warm the thermometer itself is. It shows the air's temperature only when the air is the only thing warming or cooling it.
explanations.description: In the shade, the thermometer gives heat to the air or takes heat from it until both are equally warm. Then its reading is the air's temperature. In sunlight, something else happens. The thermometer takes in sunlight, and that light warms it, on top of the air. So it climbs above the air's temperature. The air around it has not changed. Only the thermometer has. This is why a thermometer in the sun can read 5, 10 or even more degrees above one in the shade nearby.
examples: In the Sun or Shade test, a thermometer hung in the sun read 44 °C. In the shade, a metre away, it read 33 °C.
Digital temperature signs at bus stops often stand in the sun. On sunny days they can show much higher numbers than the weather report.
explanations.art: One thermometer in sunlight with little yellow arrows of light going into it, and one in shade with only the air around it.
explanations.context: This card explains the surprise in the Sun or Shade test: why one thermometer read so much higher in the sun.

explanations.concept: Why sunlight warms things more than it warms the air
explanations.definition: Clear air lets most sunlight pass straight through it. The ground, walls and other solid things take in much more sunlight, and they warm up first. The air is warmed mostly by touching the warm ground.
explanations.description: Air is see-through, so most sunlight goes through it without warming it much. When sunlight lands on a floor, a wall or a thermometer, much of it is taken in, and the thing gets warm. A dark thing takes in more light than a white or shiny thing, so it warms more. This is why a sunny wall or ledge can be too hot to touch while the air beside it feels only warm. A thermometer near a sunny wall is warmed by the wall too.
examples: At noon, a black car roof can be too hot to touch while the air beside it is only warm.
A white paper roof over a thermometer takes in less sunlight than a black one would.
explanations.art: Sunlight shining down through clear air onto a balcony floor, with the floor drawn glowing warm and the air only lightly tinted.
explanations.context: This card explains why sunny surfaces get so hot, while the air beside them stays cooler.

explanations.concept: The weather screen: a shaded house for thermometers
explanations.definition: A weather screen is a white box with slatted sides, on legs. It holds thermometers about 1.25 to 2 metres above short grass. It keeps sunlight off them and lets air flow through.
explanations.description: Every part of it has a reason. White takes in little sunlight, so the box itself stays cool. The slats let the air blow through, so the air inside is the same as the air outside. The legs keep it away from the ground, which gets hot in the day and cold at night. It stands in an open place, away from walls. The design was made in Scotland in the 1860s by Thomas Stevenson, a lighthouse engineer, so it is often called a Stevenson screen. Today almost every country follows the same rules, so a reading in Chennai can be fairly compared with one in Nairobi or Tokyo.
examples: Weather stations in India keep their thermometers in white screens on legs.
Your white paper roof in the Sun or Shade test was a very simple weather screen.
explanations.art: A white slatted box on legs, cut open to show two thermometers inside, with arrows of air blowing through the slats and sunlight bouncing off the roof.
explanations.context: This card explains how real weather stations keep the sun off their thermometers.

explanations.concept: How a rain gauge measures rain
explanations.definition: A rain gauge catches rain, and we measure the depth of water in it in millimetres. That depth is the rainfall.
explanations.description: Rain falls over a whole area. A wide container catches more water than a narrow one, but it spreads that water over a bigger floor. So, if both have straight sides, the water rises to the same depth in both. That is why the width of a rain gauge does not matter, but its shape does. A container that is narrow at the bottom and wide at the top fills deeper than the true rainfall. Many steel tumblers are like that. Real rain gauges have a funnel on top that leads into a measuring tube, which makes small amounts easy to read. One millimetre of rain on one square metre of ground is one litre of water.
examples: In the Wide or Narrow test, a steel dabba and a straight glass under the same shower both filled to about 20 mm.
If 10 mm of rain falls on a flat terrace of 50 square metres, that is 500 litres of water.
An old Indian book, the Arthashastra, describes a bowl set up in front of a storehouse as a rain gauge.
explanations.art: A wide steel dabba and a narrow straight glass side by side in the rain, with water at the same height in both and a ruler next to each.
explanations.context: This card explains how a rain gauge works, and why a wide one and a narrow one give the same reading.

explanations.definition: A wind is named for the direction it comes from. A wind vane turns until its arrow points into the wind, towards where the wind comes from.
explanations.description: A wind vane has a small arrowhead at one end and a big, flat tail at the other. The wind pushes harder on the big tail. So the vane swings round until the tail is blown away from the wind, downwind. Then the arrow points the other way, into the wind. If the arrow points west, the wind is coming from the west. In India, the big summer winds come from the southwest, over the sea, and bring the southwest monsoon. In Chennai, much of the year's rain comes in October to December, with winds from the northeast. This is called the northeast monsoon.
examples: Hold a hand fan to the east of a wind vane and wave it. The arrow turns to point east, at the fan.
An airport windsock is the other way round. Its open end faces the wind, and the sock blows away from it.
explanations.art: A wind vane on a bottle with N, E, S, W marked, a child waving a hand fan from the east, and the arrow pointing at the fan.
explanations.context: This card explains how a wind vane works, and why winds are named for where they come from.

explanations.definition: Wind speed is how fast the air is moving. An anemometer measures it. You can also judge it by eye, from what the wind does to things around you.
explanations.description: In a cup anemometer, the wind pushes the open side of each cup harder than the round back, so the cups spin. The faster they spin, the stronger the wind. Long before machines, sailors judged the wind from what they saw. In 1805, Francis Beaufort, an officer in the British navy, wrote down a scale from 0, calm, to 12, a hurricane. At first, each number was described by what the wind did to a ship's sails. Later, signs on land were added, such as smoke rising straight up or branches swaying. Weather offices still use a version of his scale.
examples: Calm: smoke rises straight up and leaves do not move.
A strong breeze: big branches sway and it is hard to hold an umbrella.
explanations.art: A row of five little pictures from calm to strong wind: still clothes, gently moving leaves, a flapping flag, swaying branches, an umbrella turned inside out.
explanations.context: This card is about measuring how strong the wind is, with a machine or with your eyes.

explanations.definition: On a clear day, the air is usually warmest in the middle of the afternoon, around 2 to 4 o'clock, not at noon. It is usually coolest just before sunrise.
explanations.description: The Sun is highest at about noon, but the air keeps warming after that. The ground and buildings keep taking in sunlight and passing warmth to the air. Until mid-afternoon, they take in more heat than they lose. After that, the Sun is lower and they lose more than they take in, so the air starts to cool. All night, heat keeps leaving, so the coolest time is just before the Sun comes back. Clouds change this. On a cloudy or rainy day, the temperature may hardly change at all.
examples: A shade thermometer in Madurai might read 28 °C at 7 in the morning, 35 °C at noon and 37 °C at 3 in the afternoon.
A pot of water on the stove keeps getting hotter for a while even after you turn the flame down a little.
explanations.art: A line chart of one day's temperature rising from dawn, peaking in mid-afternoon, and falling through the night, with a small Sun high at noon.
explanations.context: This card explains a pattern you can find in your own weather diary: when the air is warmest.

explanations.definition: The India Meteorological Department, IMD, measures and reports the weather for the whole country. It was started in 1875.
explanations.description: Every day, hundreds of IMD weather stations measure temperature, rain and wind in the same way, at the same times. Many are now automatic weather stations, which send readings by themselves. For a long time, India bought its weather instruments from abroad. Anna Mani, a scientist born in Peermade in Kerala in 1918, changed that. She joined IMD in 1948 and led the work to design and make weather instruments in India. She also measured sunlight and wind across India, to find good places for solar and wind power.
examples: Chennai's weather reports come from two stations: Nungambakkam in the city and Meenambakkam at the airport.
Thousands of rain gauges across India are read every morning, and the rain is added up for each district.
explanations.art: Anna Mani in a sari at a weather station, checking an instrument, with a white weather screen behind her.
explanations.context: This card is about who measures India's weather, and a scientist from Kerala who helped India make its own instruments.

explanations.description: Many weather apps show two numbers: the temperature, and what it 'feels like'. The first is measured with a thermometer in the shade. The second is worked out from the temperature, how damp the air is, and how windy it is. Damp air makes it harder for sweat to dry, so a humid 34 °C in Chennai can feel worse than a dry 38 °C in Jaipur. There is no single agreed way to work out the 'feels like' number. Different countries and apps use different formulas, so they can give different answers for the same weather.
examples: A weather app may say 33 °C, feels like 41 °C, on a sticky Chennai afternoon.
A fan makes you feel cooler, but it does not change what a thermometer reads.
explanations.art: A phone weather app showing '33 °C, feels like 41 °C', with a sweating child holding a hand fan.
explanations.context: This card is about a number that weather apps show, and why it is worked out rather than measured.

agreed.text: To measure the temperature of the air, a thermometer must be kept out of direct sunlight, with air flowing round it.
agreed.evidence: A thermometer in the sun reads well above one in the shade nearby. Weather offices around the world follow the same rules from the World Meteorological Organization, so their readings can be compared.

agreed.text: Rainfall is measured as a depth, in millimetres, in a container with straight sides or a funnel of known size.
agreed.evidence: Straight-sided containers of different widths under the same rain fill to the same depth. Rain gauges have been compared side by side for centuries.

agreed.text: A wind is named for the direction it comes from.
agreed.evidence: This is the rule used by weather offices, sailors and pilots everywhere, so a 'west wind' means the same thing to everyone.

agreed.text: On clear days, the air is usually warmest in the mid-afternoon and coolest just before sunrise.
agreed.evidence: Hourly readings from weather stations show this pattern on most clear days, all over the world.

challenging.claim: A thermometer on a sunny wall tells you how hot the day is.
challenging.for: It is a real thermometer, and it is outside in the weather.
challenging.against: Sunlight heats the thermometer, and the hot wall heats it too. So it reads far above the air. The Sun or Shade test shows the difference in a few minutes.
challenging.context: Where you put a thermometer changes what it says. This card is about a common mistake.

challenging.claim: A wider rain gauge measures more rain.
challenging.for: A wider container does catch more water.
challenging.against: It also spreads that water over a wider floor. With straight sides, the depth is the same. Rain is measured as depth, not as how much water was caught.
challenging.context: Does the size of a rain gauge change the answer? This card looks at a common guess.

challenging.claim: A wind vane points where the wind is going.
challenging.for: Many arrows point the way something moves.
challenging.against: A wind vane's arrow points into the wind, to where it comes from. Wave a fan at a vane, and the arrow points at the fan.
challenging.context: Which way does a wind vane point? This card is about an easy mix-up.

challenging.claim: Noon is the hottest time of the day, because the Sun is highest.
challenging.for: The sunlight is strongest at noon.
challenging.against: The ground and buildings keep warming the air for hours after noon. Shade readings through a day usually peak at about 2 to 4 in the afternoon.
challenging.context: When is the air warmest? This card checks a common belief against what thermometers show.

challenging.claim: My street is hotter than the weather report says.
challenging.who: Many people living in big cities
challenging.for: Roads, roofs and walls soak up sunlight and give off heat into the evening. Fewer trees means less shade.
challenging.against: The report gives the temperature at one weather station, often at an airport with open ground. That is a fair reading of that place, not of every street.
challenging.context: Can one number tell the temperature of a whole city? This card says why your street may really be warmer.

big_questions.q: Your thermometer gave three different numbers in three places, all in the same air. Which number was the 'real' temperature?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each number really measured: the air, the sunlight, or both.

big_questions.q: Can we ever measure something without changing it, or without the tool taking part?
big_questions.hint: A cold thermometer put into a small cup of hot tea cools the tea a tiny bit. Is that true of every measurement?

big_questions.q: Why do we need numbers for weather at all? Isn't 'hot' good enough?
big_questions.hint: Think of a farmer deciding when to sow, or a city deciding whether to store more water.

big_questions.q: The air you breathe today was over another country last week. Whose weather is it?
big_questions.hint: The southwest monsoon winds cross the Arabian Sea before they reach Kerala.

big_questions.q: A crow, a neem tree and an ant feel the weather without any tools. What do they notice that we might miss?
big_questions.hint: Watch how birds and ants behave before a rain, and on a very hot afternoon.

big_questions.q: If every home kept a weather diary, what could a whole city learn?
big_questions.hint: Some streets are hotter than others. Who would want to know that, and why?

story.title: The Balcony That Said 45
story.note: Nila, Arun, their mother and their flat are made up. The facts are real: a thermometer in the sun reads well above the air, weather reports give the shade temperature, and Chennai's readings come from stations at Nungambakkam and Meenambakkam.
text: Nila was nine, and she had a new thermometer. It was a long glass one with red liquid inside, and it came in a cardboard tube. Her aunt in Madurai had sent it for her birthday, with a note: 'For the scientist of the family.'

Nila lived on the third floor of a block of flats in Mylapore, in Chennai. The flat had one small balcony, with a grill all round it and a clothesline across the top. In the mornings the balcony was in shade. After eleven o'clock, the sun moved round and poured onto it.
On the first Saturday of May, Nila tied her thermometer to the balcony grill with a piece of thread. Then she went inside to help her mother make lemon rice.
At one o'clock, the radio in the kitchen gave the weather. 'Chennai today. Nungambakkam, maximum 36 degrees Celsius. Meenambakkam, 37 degrees.'
Nila ran to the balcony. The sun was blazing on the grill. She bent close to the thermometer and read it carefully, with her eye level with the top of the red line. It said 45.
'Amma!' she shouted. 'The radio is wrong! It is 45 degrees, not 36!'
Her little brother Arun, who was six, came running too. He looked at the red line, and then at the radio. 'Maybe our balcony is just hotter than Nungambakkam,' he said.
Their mother came out with a ladle still in her hand. She read the thermometer. 'It does say 45,' she said. 'So, Nila, who is right? Your thermometer, or the weather office?'
'Mine,' said Nila. 'I can see it.'
'Then can you show me?' said Amma. 'Not by saying it. By testing it.'

Nila thought about it all through lunch. If the balcony was really 45 degrees, then the air everywhere on the balcony should be 45 degrees. But one corner of the balcony, behind the big pot of tulsi, was still in shade.
After lunch she untied the thermometer and tied it again in the shady corner, with the same thread. She waited, and she made Arun wait too, for five whole minutes. Then she read it. 35.
'It went down by ten!' said Arun. 'The corner is colder.'

Nila frowned. The two places were only a metre apart. The same air blew across the whole balcony. She could feel it on her arms. It did not feel ten degrees different. But her arms in the sunny part felt hot, as if the sunlight itself was pressing on them.

Then she had an idea. She took a sheet of white paper from her school bag and folded it in half, like a little roof. She tied the thermometer back in the sunny spot, and taped the paper roof to the grill just above it. Now the thermometer hung in the sun's place, in the sun's air, but in the paper's shadow.
Five minutes later, she read it. 36.
Arun stared. 'The paper made the air cold?'

'No,' said Nila slowly. 'The air is the same air. The paper only stopped the sunlight landing on the thermometer.' She looked at the glass tube. 'When the sun shone on it, the sunlight was heating the thermometer itself. It was telling me how hot the thermometer was.'
'So is it 45 or 36?' asked Arun.
'The air is about 36,' said Nila. 'The thermometer in the sun was 45. They are both true. They are just about different things.'
Amma smiled. 'And the weather office?'
'They must keep their thermometers in the shade,' said Nila. 'Otherwise every town would get a different number depending on where the sun was.'

That evening, her mother showed her a picture on her phone. It was a white wooden box with slatted sides, standing on legs on a patch of grass. 'This is a weather screen,' she said. 'Weather stations keep their thermometers inside one. The white keeps the sunlight off. The slats let the air through.'
'It's my paper roof,' said Nila, 'only better.'
The next morning, Nila made a new page in her notebook. At the top she wrote 'Weather Diary'. Underneath she drew a table: Date. Time. Temperature in the shade. Sky. Wind.
And next to the word 'Temperature' she added a small note to herself, in red pencil: 'Shade only.'
story.epiphany: A thermometer in the sun was heating up in the sunlight, so it showed its own temperature, not the air's. In the shade, the air was the only thing warming it, so it showed the air's temperature.
ask: Why did Nila's thermometer read 45 in the sun and 36 under the paper roof, in the same air?
Arun thought the shady corner was colder. What did Nila do to test that idea?
Why did Amma ask Nila to test it, instead of just telling her the answer?
Where would you hang a thermometer in your home to measure the air?

games.title: Weather Station Match
games.context: This is a card game. You match each weather question to the right tool, and spot the mistakes that would give a wrong reading.

printables.title: 16 question cards to cut out
items: How warm is the air this afternoon? (Thermometer)
How much rain fell last night? (Rain gauge)
Where is the wind coming from? (Wind vane)
How fast is the wind blowing? (Anemometer)
Is the monsoon wind here yet, from the southwest? (Wind vane)
Did more rain fall this week than last week? (Rain gauge)

MISTAKE: Arjun hangs his thermometer in full sun. What goes wrong? (It reads too high. Move it to the shade.)
MISTAKE: Meena puts her rain gauge under the balcony roof. What goes wrong? (It catches no rain. Put it under open sky.)
MISTAKE: Divya's rain gauge is a tumbler that is narrow at the bottom. What goes wrong? (It fills deeper than the true rain. Use straight sides.)
MISTAKE: Farhan's wind vane has a big arrowhead and a tiny tail. What goes wrong? (It won't turn to face the wind. Make the tail bigger.)
MISTAKE: Priya's thermometer touches a sunny wall. What goes wrong? (The hot wall warms it. Hang it in the air.)
MISTAKE: Revathi reads her rain gauge only once a week in May. What goes wrong? (Some water evaporates. Read it every day.)

TEST IT: Point to where the wind is coming from. Check with your wind vane.

printables.title: A score sheet with each player's name and 16 boxes

rules: Lay the 4 tool cards face up. Shuffle the question cards face down.
On your turn, turn over a question card and read it aloud.
For a question, put it on the right tool. Right: score 1 point.
For a MISTAKE card, say what goes wrong and how to fix it. Right: score 2 points.
For a TEST IT card, do the test. Everyone who guessed well scores 1 point.
Check answers in the brackets. Playing alone? Try to beat your own score next time.
The player with the most points when the cards run out wins.

check.q: Arjun hangs his thermometer in full sun. What goes wrong?
options: It reads too high, because sunlight heats it
check.why: Sunlight heats the thermometer itself, so it shows more than the air's temperature. Weather stations keep thermometers in the shade for this reason.

experiments.title: Sun or Shade: where does a thermometer tell the truth about the air?
experiments.question: Does a thermometer give the same reading in the sun, in the shade, and in the sun under a white paper roof? Which one shows the temperature of the air?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the thermometer read the same in all three places, or different? Which place will read highest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same thermometer, hung from the same thread, at the same height, in places less than two metres apart. Wait the same 5 minutes in each place before reading. Only the sunlight changes. If you can, do the whole test again the next day at the same time, because one day can be a fluke.

materials.item: a thermometer that reads up to at least 60 °C: a laboratory thermometer with red liquid, or a digital thermometer with a probe. A fever thermometer will not work, because it reads only a small range near body temperature.
a piece of thread or string, about 30 cm long
a sheet of white A4 paper and some sticky tape
a balcony or a window grill with a sunny spot and a shady spot close together
a phone with a weather app, or today's newspaper weather box
a phone timer or a clock

experiments.safety: A glass thermometer breaks easily. Tie it firmly, and keep it away from the edge of the balcony. If it breaks, a grown-up sweeps up the glass. Never look at the Sun.

schedule.what: Guess. Read the thermometer in the shade, in the sun, and in the sun under a white paper roof. Compare with the weather report.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw your balcony or window from above, and mark the three places with their readings.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the thermometer. 2. Show the sunny spot and the shady spot. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason for each of the three places.
flow.say: We will hang the thermometer in three places: in the shade, in the sun, and in the sun under a paper roof. What will it read in each? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the sunny spot and the shady spot. Guess the reading in each place. Why do you think so?

ask.q: Will the thermometer read the same everywhere on the balcony?
good: Any guess with a reason is good, for example 'It will be higher in the sun because the sun is hot.'

flow.parent: Don't explain anything yet. Write down your child's three guesses. The best time is late morning or early afternoon on a sunny day, when part of the balcony or window is in full sun. No thermometer yet? A straw thermometer, a bottle of coloured water with a straw in it, shows the same change as a rising level, without degrees.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sun or Shade test. You guess what a thermometer will read in three places.

flow.do: 1. Fold the white A4 sheet in half, like a roof. 2. Keep it ready with two pieces of tape. 3. Tie the thread round the top of the thermometer.
flow.say: This paper roof will make a shadow. We'll use it in the third test.
flow.kid: Fold the white paper in half like a roof. Tie the thread to the thermometer.
flow.parent: With a digital probe thermometer, hang the probe tip in the air, not touching anything. Keep the display box in the shade if you can.

flow.do: 1. Tie the thermometer to the grill in the shady spot. 2. It must hang in the air, touching nothing. 3. Wait 5 minutes. 4. Read it, then read again 1 minute later. 5. Write both readings.
flow.say: We read it twice, a minute apart. If both are the same, the thermometer has finished warming or cooling.
flow.kid: Hang the thermometer in the shade. Don't let it touch the wall. Wait 5 minutes. Read it. Read it again after 1 minute.
flow.parent: Read with your eye level with the top of the red line, not from above or below. If the second reading is still changing, wait another minute. Touching the wall or the grill would let them warm the thermometer, which is why it must hang free.

check.q: Why do we read the thermometer twice, a minute apart?
options: To check it has stopped changing
Because the first reading is always wrong
To make the test take longer
check.why: A thermometer takes a few minutes to become as warm as its surroundings. When two readings a minute apart are the same, it has finished changing. Picking 'always wrong' means thinking the tool is broken. It is not. It is only slow.

flow.do: 1. Move the thermometer to the sunny spot, less than two metres away, at the same height. 2. Again it hangs in the air, touching nothing. 3. Wait 5 minutes. 4. Read it twice, a minute apart.
flow.say: Same thermometer, same thread, same height. Only the sunlight is different. What does it say now?
flow.kid: Hang it in the sun now. Same height. Wait 5 minutes. Read it twice. Was your guess right?
flow.parent: Expect a much higher reading, often 5 to 15 degrees above the shade. If it climbs near the top of its scale, take it out of the sun. On a cloudy day the difference is small: try again on a sunny day.

flow.do: 1. Leave the thermometer hanging in the sun. 2. Tape the paper roof to the grill just above it, so it hangs in the roof's shadow. 3. Leave both ends of the roof open for air. 4. Wait 5 minutes. 5. Read it twice.
flow.say: Now the thermometer is in the same sunny air, but the paper stops sunlight landing on it. What do you think it will read?
flow.kid: Tape the paper roof above the thermometer. It is in the shadow now. Wait 5 minutes. Read it twice.
flow.parent: The reading usually falls back to within a degree or three of the shade reading. It may stay a little higher, because the paper itself warms up in the sun.

check.q: The thermometer in the sun read 44 °C. Under the paper roof, in the same spot, it read 35 °C. What did the paper roof change?
options: It stopped sunlight landing on the thermometer
It blew cool air onto the thermometer
check.why: The air around the thermometer was the same air. The paper only blocked the sunlight that was heating the thermometer itself. Picking 'made the air colder' is a natural guess, but the paper roof was open at both ends, and the air flowed right through.

flow.do: 1. Open a weather app, or look at today's newspaper weather box. 2. Find the temperature for your town right now. 3. Compare it with your three readings.
flow.say: Weather stations measure the air in the shade. Which of our three readings is closest to the weather report?
flow.kid: Look at the weather app. Which of your readings is closest to it?

check.q: Which of your readings is likely to be closest to the weather report?
options: The one in the shade, or under the paper roof
None of them could ever be close
check.why: Weather stations keep their thermometers in a white shaded box, so they measure the air. Your shade and paper-roof readings were made the same way. Your street may still be a degree or two different from the weather station, which is often at an airport.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a thermometer in the sun reads too high, so to measure the air it must be in the shade. What I saw: it read 33 °C in the shade, 44 °C in the sun and 35 °C in the sun under the paper roof. Why: sunlight heats the thermometer itself, so in the sun it shows its own warmth, not the air's.

experiments.context: In this experiment you hang one thermometer in three places on your balcony or window: in the shade, in the sun, and in the sun under a white paper roof. You find out which reading is the temperature of the air.

experiments.title: Wide or Narrow: does a bigger rain gauge catch deeper rain?
experiments.question: If a wide container and a narrow container stand side by side in the same rain, which one fills deeper?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which will have the deeper water, the wide one or the narrow one, or will they be the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both containers have straight sides and stand side by side, the same distance from the middle of the shower. They get the same 'rain' for the same time. Then swap their places and do it again, because the spray may be heavier on one side.

materials.item: a wide container with straight sides, such as a steel dabba or a plastic tub
a narrow container with straight sides, such as a straight glass or a plastic jar
a ruler with millimetre marks
a shower in the bathroom. No shower? A steel chalni or a watering can, and a bucket of water with a mug.
a bucket, to save the water for mopping or plants

experiments.safety: Bathroom floors get slippery. Wear chappals and move slowly. Glass containers can break: use plastic or steel if you can.

schedule.what: Make rain with a shower over a wide and a narrow container. Measure the depth in each, swap them, and do it again.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the two containers side by side, with the water level in each.

flow.do: 1. Show both containers. 2. Check that each one is as wide at the top as at the bottom. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Rain will fall on both of these for one minute. Which one will have the deeper water? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the wide one and the narrow one. Which will fill deeper? Why?
flow.parent: Many steel tumblers are narrower at the bottom than at the top. Those fill deeper than the true rain, so don't use them. Write down your child's guess before you start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wide or Narrow test. You guess whether a wide or a narrow rain gauge fills deeper.

flow.do: 1. Stand both containers side by side on the bathroom floor. 2. Put them the same distance from the spot right under the shower. 3. Turn the shower on for exactly 1 minute. 4. Turn it off.
flow.say: This is our rain. Both containers stand in the same rain for the same minute.
flow.kid: Put both side by side under the shower. Turn it on for 1 minute. Then turn it off.
flow.parent: No shower? Hold a steel chalni high over both containers. Pour three mugs of water through it, moving it slowly back and forth over both. Afterwards, pour the water into the bucket and use it for mopping.

flow.do: 1. Stand the ruler straight up inside each container, touching the bottom. 2. Read the depth of the water in millimetres. 3. Write both depths.
flow.say: Look at where your ruler's 0 is. Many rulers have a little gap before the 0, so we line up the 0 with the bottom.
flow.kid: Stand the ruler in each one. Read how deep the water is, in millimetres. Write it down.

check.q: The wide dabba and the narrow glass both have water about 20 mm deep. Which one caught more water?
check.why: The wide dabba caught more water, because more rain fell on its wider opening. But it spread that water over a wider floor, so the depth came out the same. Picking 'the same amount' mixes up how deep the water is with how much water there is.

flow.do: 1. Empty both containers into the bucket. 2. Swap their places. 3. Run the shower for 1 minute again. 4. Measure both depths again.
flow.say: Maybe the shower sprays more on one side. If we swap them and get the same answer, we can trust it.
flow.kid: Empty them. Swap their places. Shower for 1 minute again. Measure again.
flow.parent: The two depths are usually within a few millimetres of each other. A bigger difference usually means the spray is uneven, which is why we swap and repeat.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a wide and a narrow container fill to the same depth in the same rain, as long as both have straight sides. What I saw: the dabba and the glass both had about 20 mm of water, both times. Why: the wide one catches more rain but spreads it over a bigger floor, so the depth is the same. That is why rain is measured as a depth.

experiments.context: In this experiment you make rain with a shower over a wide container and a narrow one. You find out whether the size of a rain gauge changes the reading.

experiments.title: When Is the Air Warmest? One day of readings
experiments.question: At what time of day is the air warmest, and at what time is it coolest?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the air be warmest at noon, when the Sun is highest, or at some other time? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same thermometer in the same shaded place all day, under the white paper roof if the sun reaches it. Wait 5 minutes before each reading. Only the time of day changes. Choose a clear day if you can, because clouds and rain change the pattern.

materials.item: the thermometer from the Sun or Shade test
thread, and the white paper roof from the Sun or Shade test
a notebook, a pencil and a clock

experiments.safety: Tie the glass thermometer firmly, away from the balcony edge.

schedule.what: Read the shade thermometer at 7 in the morning, 10, 12 noon, 2, 4 and 7 in the evening. Draw a line chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a line chart, with the times along the bottom and the temperature up the side.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess: at what time will the air be warmest, and why? 2. Hang the thermometer in the shade, under the paper roof. 3. Write the times in the table.
flow.say: Today we read the thermometer six times, from morning to evening. When do you think it will be warmest? Why?
flow.kid: When will the air be warmest today? Guess, and say why. Write the times in your table.
flow.parent: Most children guess noon. Don't correct them. The readings will answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of a day of readings. You guess when the air will be warmest, then measure it.

flow.do: At 7, 10, 12, 2, 4 and 7 o'clock: 1. Wait until the thermometer has been in place 5 minutes. 2. Read it. 3. Write the time, the reading and the sky.
flow.say: It's reading time. What does it say now? Is it higher or lower than last time?
flow.kid: Read the thermometer. Write the time and the number. Is the sky sunny or cloudy?
flow.wait: Read it six times through the day
flow.parent: Each reading takes about two minutes. If you miss one, write 'missed'. Don't guess a number.

flow.do: 1. Draw a line chart: times along the bottom, temperature up the side. 2. Put a dot for each reading and join the dots. 3. Circle the highest dot.
flow.say: Let's see the whole day at once. Where is the highest point on our chart?
flow.kid: Draw a dot for each reading. Join them. Circle the highest one. What time was it?

check.q: On a clear day, when is the shade temperature usually highest?
options: In the middle of the afternoon
check.why: The ground and buildings keep taking in sunlight and warming the air for hours after noon. Until mid-afternoon they gain more heat than they lose. Picking 'at noon' makes sense, because the sunlight is strongest then, but the air takes time to catch up.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the air is warmest in the afternoon, not at noon. What I saw: it was 28 °C at 7, 34 °C at noon and 36 °C at 2, then it went down to 31 °C by 7 in the evening. Why: the ground and walls keep warming the air after noon, until the Sun gets low.

experiments.context: In this experiment you read a shaded thermometer six times in one day, and find out when the air is warmest and coolest.

flow.say: Let's be weather watchers with no tools at all. What is the weather doing right now? How can you tell?
flow.kid: Go to the window. Is it warm or cool? Windy or still? Cloudy or clear? How do you know?

ask.q: How can you tell if it is windy without going outside?
good: The clothes on the line are moving.
The leaves on the tree are swaying.

flow.say: If you had to give it a number, how many degrees is the air right now? What makes that hard to guess?
flow.kid: Guess how many degrees the air is. Write it down. Is it easy to guess?
flow.parent: Most guesses are a few degrees off. That is the point: our skin is not a measuring tool. Keep the guess for the Sun or Shade test.

activities.title: Make a Wind Vane

materials.item: a drinking straw
thin card, such as a cereal box
a straight pin
a pencil with an eraser on the end
a small plastic bottle, half filled with water or sand, so it does not tip over
sticky tape, scissors and a marker
a phone compass, to find north
a hand fan or a folded newspaper

activities.safety: A grown-up pushes the pin in. Keep the pin point away from faces.

schedule.what: Make the wind vane. Test it with a fan. Mark N, E, S and W. Put it on the balcony.

activities.record: Draw your wind vane. Write where the wind was coming from.

flow.do: 1. Cut a small triangle, about 3 cm, for the arrowhead. 2. Cut a bigger shape, about 6 cm, for the tail. 3. Cut a short slit at each end of the straw. 4. Slide the arrowhead in one end and the tail in the other.
flow.say: The tail must be bigger than the arrowhead. We'll see why when we test it.
flow.kid: Cut a small arrowhead and a big tail from card. Slide them into the ends of the straw.
flow.context: This is the first step of making a wind vane. You make the arrow from a straw and card.

flow.do: 1. Find the balance point of the straw on your finger. 2. Push the pin through the straw there. 3. Push the pin into the pencil's eraser. 4. Check the straw spins easily.
flow.say: The straw must spin freely, or the wind can't turn it.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to push the pin through the straw and into the eraser. Spin it. Does it turn easily?
flow.parent: If it sticks, make the hole in the straw a little bigger by wiggling the pin. Stand the pencil in the bottle neck. Wrap tape round the pencil if it is loose.

flow.do: 1. Stand the vane on a table. 2. Wave the fan at it from one side. 3. See where the arrow points. 4. Move to another side and wave again.
flow.say: Where does the arrow point: towards the fan, or away from it?
flow.kid: Wave the fan at your vane. Where does the arrow point? Try from another side.

check.q: You wave a fan at the wind vane from the east. Where does the arrow point?
check.why: The wind pushes harder on the big tail, so the tail swings away from the wind. That turns the arrow to face into the wind, towards where it comes from. Picking 'away from the fan' is the most common mix-up: arrows usually point the way things move.

flow.do: 1. Use the phone compass to find north. 2. Write N, E, S and W on the bottle in the right places. 3. Put the vane on the balcony ledge or a window sill, open to the wind. 4. Read where the wind is coming from.
flow.say: Winds are named for where they come from. If the arrow points to the S, it is a south wind.
flow.kid: Find north with the phone. Write N, E, S and W on the bottle. Put it outside. Where is the wind coming from?
flow.parent: Walls and buildings bend the wind in a city, so a balcony vane may swing about. Watch it for a minute and write the direction it points most often. Keep the phone half a metre from metal grills when finding north.

activities.title: How Strong Is the Wind? Read it from the window

activities.record: Write today's wind number, and what you saw that told you.

flow.do: Copy this card into the notebook. 0: Calm. Nothing moves. 1: Light. Leaves just move. 2: Gentle. Clothes on the line sway. 3: Breezy. Small branches move and a flag flaps. 4: Strong. Big branches sway. 5: Very strong. It's hard to hold an umbrella.
flow.say: Long ago, sailors judged the wind by what it did. We can do that too, with this card.
flow.kid: Copy the wind card. 0 is calm. 5 is very strong.

flow.say: What can you see moving? Which number on the card fits best?
flow.kid: Look out for one minute. What is moving? Which number fits?

check.q: From her window in Kochi, Lakshmi sees coconut leaves swaying and big branches moving. Which number fits best?
check.why: Big branches swaying means a strong wind. In light wind only the leaves move a little. A strong answer looks at the biggest thing the wind is moving.

activities.context: In this activity you judge how strong the wind is, using only your eyes and a simple card.

your notebook

schedule.what: Find the maximum, the minimum and the rainfall for your town. Compare them with your own readings.

activities.record: Write your town's maximum, minimum and rainfall for yesterday. Write your own reading next to them.

flow.do: 1. Open the weather box or app. 2. Find your town. 3. Point to the maximum temperature, the minimum temperature and the rainfall in millimetres. 4. Write them down.
flow.say: This is what weather stations measured yesterday. Max means the highest temperature. Min means the lowest.
flow.kid: Find your town. Find the max, the min and the rain. Write them down.
flow.context: This is the first step of reading a weather report. You find the main numbers and what they mean.

flow.do: 1. Ask: at what time of day was the max probably measured? And the min? 2. Compare the report with your own shade reading.
flow.say: When do you think the air was warmest yesterday? When was it coolest? Is our reading close to the report?
flow.kid: When was it warmest? When was it coolest? Is your reading close to the report?

ask.q: Why might our reading be a little different from the report?
good: The weather station is in a different place.
Our street has more walls and roads.
We measured at a different time.

flow.parent: The max is usually in the afternoon and the min just before sunrise. A difference of a degree or two from your own shade reading is normal.

activities.title: Hot Ledge, Warm Air: what does the sun heat most?

materials.item: a sunny balcony ledge, floor or window sill, and a shaded one

activities.safety: Sunny surfaces can be very hot in summer. A grown-up tests first. Touch only for a moment, with the back of your hand.

schedule.what: Feel a sunny surface, a shaded surface and the air above each, with the back of your hand.

activities.record: Write the four places in order, from hottest to coolest.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up touches the sunny ledge first, to check it is safe. 2. Your child touches it for a moment with the back of the hand. 3. Then holds the hand in the air just above it.
flow.say: Which feels hotter, the sunny ledge or the air just above it? Why might that be?
flow.kid: Touch the sunny ledge for a moment. Now hold your hand just above it. Which feels hotter?
flow.context: This is the first step of finding what sunlight heats most: solid things or the air.

flow.do: 1. Do the same on a shaded ledge or floor. 2. Put the four places in order from hottest to coolest.
flow.say: Sunlight goes straight through clear air, but the ledge takes it in. What does that tell us about where to put a thermometer?
flow.kid: Now feel a shady ledge and the air above it. Put all four in order, hottest first.

check.q: Why does a sunny ledge get hotter than the air just above it?
options: Clear air lets most sunlight pass through, but the ledge takes it in
The ledge is closer to the Sun
check.why: Sunlight passes through clear air without warming it much. The ledge takes in the light and heats up, and then it warms the air touching it. That is why a thermometer must not touch a sunny wall or ledge. The ledge is not really closer to the Sun in any way that matters.

activities.context: In this activity you feel which gets hotter in the sun: a solid ledge or the air above it.

setup.art: A child touching a sunny balcony ledge with the back of her hand, a grown-up beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Touch the sunny ledge for a moment. Then feel the air above it.

setup.art: The child touching a shaded ledge, with arrows showing the order hottest to coolest in a notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Do the same in the shade. Put them in order.

projects.title: My Weather Diary: one week

materials.item: the thermometer and the white paper roof from the Sun or Shade test
a straight-sided plastic jar or steel dabba, for a rain gauge, and a ruler
the wind vane from the Make a Wind Vane activity
a notebook and coloured pencils

projects.safety: Don't go out to read the tools in a thunderstorm. Read them when it is safe. Tie the glass thermometer firmly.

schedule.what: Set up the weather station: shade thermometer, rain gauge and wind vane. Draw the diary table. Make the first entry.
Morning and afternoon readings: temperature, rain, wind and sky.
Last readings. Draw a bar chart of the afternoon temperatures. Find one pattern.

projects.record: Each day at 8 in the morning and 3 in the afternoon: the temperature in the shade, the rain in mm, where the wind comes from, the wind number from 0 to 5, and a drawing of the sky.

flow.do: 1. Hang the thermometer in the shade, under the paper roof. 2. Put the rain gauge on the open edge of the balcony or terrace, with nothing above it. 3. Put the wind vane beside it. 4. Draw the diary table and make the first entry.
flow.say: This is our own weather station. Real weather stations read their tools at the same times every day, so we will too.
flow.kid: Set up your thermometer, rain gauge and wind vane. Draw your table. Write today's weather.
flow.parent: If your balcony has a roof over all of it, the rain gauge will catch nothing. Put it on a terrace or a window ledge open to the sky, or simply write 'not measured' for rain.
flow.context: This is the first day of My Weather Diary, a 7-day project. You set up your own small weather station.

flow.do: Every morning at 8 and every afternoon at 3: 1. Read the thermometer. 2. Read the rain gauge in mm, then empty it. 3. Read the wind vane and the wind number. 4. Draw the sky.
flow.say: What does our weather station say today? Is it the same as yesterday?
flow.kid: Read your tools. Write the numbers. Empty the rain gauge. Draw the sky.
flow.wait: Do this every day for 6 days
flow.parent: No rain all week is a real result. Write 0 mm each day. A dry week in summer is normal in much of India.

flow.do: 1. Draw a bar chart of the six afternoon temperatures. 2. Ask your child to find one pattern. 3. Ask what they would like to measure next.
flow.say: Look at the whole week. What do you notice? Was it always warmer in the afternoon? Did the wind usually come from one side?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each afternoon. What pattern can you see?

check.q: In Kavya's diary, the afternoon was warmer than the morning on all seven days. What is the best thing to say?
options: Afternoons are always warmer, everywhere, forever
In this week, at her home, afternoons were warmer than mornings
check.why: One week at one home shows a pattern for that week and that place. To say more, you would need more weeks and more places. That is why weather stations keep records for many years.

projects.context: In this 7-day project you keep a weather diary, with your own thermometer, rain gauge and wind vane, and look for patterns.

setup.caption: 2. Read them at 8 and at 3 every day. Write it down.

setup.caption: 3. On day 7, draw a bar chart. Find a pattern.

challenges.title: A Weather Screen for Your Balcony
challenges.problem: A paper roof keeps the sun off a thermometer, but wind can blow it away and the paper itself warms up. Design a better weather screen, a shaded house for your thermometer, from things at home.
constraints: Sunlight must never land on the thermometer.
Air must be able to flow through.
Its reading in the sun must be within 2 degrees of a reading in full shade.
materials: a cardboard box or a plastic food tub
scissors, used by a grown-up, and tape
general: Cut slots in the sides of a white box, so air can pass but sunlight cannot shine straight in.
Make a double roof from two sheets with a gap between them, so the top sheet gets hot but the bottom one stays cool.
Cover the outside with white paper or foil, which take in little sunlight.
creative: Use an upside-down plastic tub with holes punched in the sides, covered in white paper.
Stack three white paper plates with gaps between them, like the screens some weather stations use for small sensors.
Hang the screen from the grill, so it does not touch the hot ledge.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own weather screen. Draw it, build it, and test it: hang the thermometer inside it in the sun, then in full shade. How close are the two readings?

flow.do: 1. Hang the thermometer under the plain paper roof in the sun. 2. Read it after 5 minutes. 3. Write it down. 4. Read the shade spot too.
flow.say: This is the reading to beat. How close is the paper roof to the shade?
flow.kid: Read the thermometer under the paper roof. Then read it in the shade. How far apart are they?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Weather Screen challenge. You find out how well the plain paper roof works.

flow.do: 1. Draw a design. 2. Build it from home things. 3. A grown-up does any cutting.
flow.say: What will keep the sunlight off, but let the air through?
flow.kid: Draw your weather screen. Build it. Ask a grown-up to do the cutting.

flow.do: 1. Hang the thermometer inside your screen, in the sun. 2. Wait 5 minutes and read it. 3. Compare with the shade reading.
flow.say: Is your screen better than the paper roof? How could you make it better still?
flow.kid: Test your screen in the sun. Compare with the shade. Did you beat the paper roof?

challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You design a shaded house for a thermometer that keeps the sunlight off but lets the air through.

setup.caption: 1. Test the plain paper roof first.

setup.caption: 2. Build a better screen with slots for air.

setup.caption: 3. Test it in the sun. Compare with the shade.

challenges.title: Rain While You Are Away
challenges.problem: In hot weather, water in an open rain gauge evaporates before you read it. Evaporate means the water slowly turns into an invisible gas and goes into the air. Design a rain gauge that loses as little water as possible in one day.
constraints: Rain must still be able to get in.
Test it with 20 mm of water poured in, left on the balcony for one day.
materials: the top of a plastic bottle, to use as a funnel
general: Put a funnel in the top, so the water sits below a narrow opening and less air reaches it.
Keep the gauge in an open place but read it early in the morning, before the day's heat.
creative: Pour a thin layer of cooking oil on the water. Oil floats and slows evaporation. Some real rain gauges that are read only once a month do this.
Wrap the jar in white paper, so the sun warms it less, but leave the ruler marks visible.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to stop the rain gauge drying out. Set up two jars with 20 mm of water: one plain and one with your idea. Leave both on the balcony for a day. Which one lost less?

flow.do: 1. Pour 20 mm of water into each jar. 2. Leave one plain. 3. Add your idea to the other.
flow.say: Both start with the same water. Only your idea is different. That makes it a fair test.
flow.kid: Pour 20 mm of water into each jar. Leave one plain. Add your idea to the other.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rain While You Are Away challenge. You set up a plain jar and your improved jar.

flow.do: 1. Put both jars side by side on a sunny ledge. 2. Leave them for one day.
flow.say: Which one do you think will lose more water? Why?
flow.kid: Put both jars in the sun. Leave them for a day.

flow.do: 1. Measure the water in each jar. 2. Work out how much each lost. 3. Talk about how to make it even better.
flow.say: How many millimetres did each jar lose? Did your idea work?
flow.kid: Measure both jars. Which lost less water? Why?

challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You design a rain gauge that keeps its water from evaporating before you read it.
