quiz.p: Ishita, a girl in Class 3 in Pune, hangs one thermometer in the sun and one in the shade, a metre apart. Which reads higher?
quiz.why: Sunlight heats the thermometer in the sun, so it reads higher than the air. Picking 'the same' means thinking a thermometer only feels the air.

quiz.p: What does a thermometer in the shade show?
quiz.why: In the shade, only the air warms or cools the thermometer, so it shows the air's temperature.

quiz.p: Swathi covers her sunny thermometer with a white paper roof, open at both ends. The reading drops from 44 °C to 35 °C. Why?
opts: The paper stopped sunlight landing on the thermometer
The paper made the air colder
quiz.why: The air flowing through was the same. Only the sunlight on the thermometer was blocked.

quiz.p: In the Sun or Shade test, why do we keep the thermometer at the same height and the same thread each time?
opts: So that only the sunlight changes, and the test is fair
quiz.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Here that thing is the sunlight.

quiz.p: Rain fills a narrow straight glass to 15 mm. A wide straight dabba stands next to it. How deep is the water in the dabba?
quiz.why: Straight-sided containers fill to the same depth in the same rain. The dabba holds more water, at the same depth.
Rain is measured as the depth of water it makes, in millimetres. That way, any straight-sided gauge gives the same answer.

quiz.p: A wind vane's arrow points north. What is the wind called?
opts: A north wind, coming from the north
quiz.why: A vane points into the wind, to where it comes from. Winds are named for where they come from.

quiz.p: Why does a wind vane need a big tail?
opts: The wind pushes harder on it, turning the arrow to face the wind
quiz.why: The wind pushes the bigger surface more, so the tail swings downwind and the arrow points into the wind.

quiz.p: In a weather diary, the shade temperature on a clear day is usually highest at...
quiz.why: The ground and buildings keep warming the air after noon. Picking noon is the common guess.

quiz.p: Kavya writes '0 mm' in her weather diary on a dry day. Is that useful?
opts: Yes, a dry day is a real reading
No, she should guess a number
quiz.why: A dry day is part of the record. Leaving it out would make the week look wetter than it was.

quiz.p: In Korea in 1441, how did the crown prince improve on digging into wet soil to measure rain?
opts: He measured rain in a metal vessel with a ruler
quiz.why: A vessel soaks up nothing, so its water depth shows only the rain. Soil soaks up different amounts depending on how dry it was.

quiz.p: A weather report for Madurai says 'Max 38, Min 27'. What does 'Min 27' mean?
opts: The lowest air temperature that day was 27 °C
quiz.why: Min is the minimum, the lowest temperature of the day, usually just before sunrise.

items.p: Meenakshi wants to measure how warm the air is on her balcony. Where should she hang her thermometer?
opts: In the shade, hanging in the air
In full sun, on the wall
items.why: In the shade, with air all round it, the air is the only thing warming the thermometer, so it shows the air's temperature. In the sun, or touching a hot wall, it is heated by more than the air.

items.p: A thermometer in the sun shows the temperature of the air.
items.why: False. In the sun, the thermometer is heated by sunlight as well as by the air, so it reads higher than the air. A strong answer says it shows its own temperature, which the sunlight has raised.

items.p: Temperature is measured in degrees ____.
items.why: Degrees Celsius, written °C. Water freezes at 0 °C and boils at about 100 °C.

items.p: Match each tool to what it measures.
items.why: Each part of the weather needs its own tool. A strong answer could also say where each tool should be placed.

items.p: Farhan's wind vane points east. Where is the wind coming from?
items.why: A wind vane points into the wind, to where it comes from. So it is an east wind. Picking 'west' is the common mix-up of thinking the arrow shows where the wind is going.

items.p: Nila's thermometer read 45 °C in the sun and 36 °C under a paper roof in the same spot. Explain why.
items.a: The paper roof stopped sunlight landing on the thermometer. In the sun, the sunlight heated the thermometer itself, so it read higher than the air. Under the roof, only the air warmed it, so it showed the air's temperature.
items.why: A strong answer says the air was the same in both places, and that sunlight heated the thermometer, not the air.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3 in Mysuru, is setting up a weather station on her terrace. Sort these places for her thermometer.
items: hanging in the shade of the water tank, touching nothing
lying on the hot terrace floor
inside a white box with slatted sides
next to the kitchen exhaust fan
under a white paper roof, open at both ends
items.why: Good places keep sunlight off and let the air flow round the thermometer, and keep it away from hot walls, floors and kitchen air. A strong answer gives a reason for each bad place.

items.p: Rain falls for one hour. A wide bucket and a narrow jar, both with straight sides, stand side by side. What will you find?
opts: The water is about the same depth in both
items.why: With straight sides, both fill to the same depth. The bucket catches more water, but spreads it over a wider floor. That is why rain is measured as a depth.

items.p: Rain is measured in ____, a small unit of length. Ten of them make one centimetre.
items.why: Millimetres, written mm. A heavy shower might give 10 to 20 mm of rain.

items.p: Draw a wind vane. Label the arrowhead, the tail and the pin it turns on. Draw an arrow to show the wind coming from the west.
items.a: A vane with a small arrowhead, a bigger tail and a pin. The wind arrow comes from the west, and the vane's arrowhead points west, into the wind.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the tail is bigger, and that the arrowhead points to where the wind comes from.
items.art: A blank space with N, E, S and W marked at the edges.

items.p: Put the steps of the Sun or Shade test in order.
items: Read the thermometer in the sun
Read the thermometer in the shade
Guess the three readings, and say why
Read it under the white paper roof in the sun
a: Guess the three readings, and say why
Read the thermometer in the shade
Read the thermometer in the sun
Read it under the white paper roof in the sun
items.why: First guess, then measure in the shade, then in the sun, then in the sun with the roof. Guessing first lets the test answer your question.

items.p: Three of these are weather tools. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: A weighing scale measures weight. The other three measure parts of the weather: rain, wind direction and temperature.

items.p: Two friends in Hyderabad argue about where to put the rain gauge for their school weather diary.

views.says: Put it on the open terrace. Then all the rain can fall in.
Put it on the classroom window sill under the sunshade. Then it won't blow over, and we can read it every day.

items.ask: Whose idea gives a truer reading? Use what you know about rain gauges. Then say one good point the other friend made.
items.a: A strong answer picks Sneha for a truer reading, because a gauge under a sunshade catches little or no rain. It also gives Rohan his due: a gauge must not blow over, and it must be easy to read every day. A good answer joins both: put it on the open terrace, and weigh it down or tape it in place.
items.why: Both care about something real: getting all the rain, and making the gauge safe and easy to read. The best plan meets both needs.

items.p: Why do weather stations all follow the same rules for where to put their thermometers?
items.a: So that their readings can be compared. If one station put its thermometer in the sun and another in the shade, their numbers would be different even in the same weather.
items.why: A strong answer says that the same method makes readings from different places and days fair to compare.

items.p: Label the parts of this weather screen: the white paint, the slatted sides, the legs, the thermometer inside.
items.why: White takes in little sunlight. The slats let air through. The legs keep it away from the hot ground. The thermometer inside is shaded. A strong answer says what each part is for.
items.art: A white box with slatted sides on four legs, cut open to show a thermometer, with four empty label lines.

items.p: Lakshmi lives in Kochi. At 7 in the morning her shade thermometer reads 26 °C. At noon it reads 31 °C. What will it most likely read at 3 in the afternoon on a clear day?
items.why: On a clear day the air keeps warming after noon, until the middle of the afternoon. So it will probably be a little warmer than at noon. 50 °C is far too high for shade air in Kochi.

items.p: Arun thinks noon is the hottest time of day, because the Sun is highest then. Explain what really happens, and how you could test it.
items.a: The ground and walls keep taking in sunlight and warming the air after noon, so the air is usually warmest at about 2 to 4 in the afternoon. To test it, read a shade thermometer every two hours through a clear day and find the highest reading.
items.why: A strong answer gives the reason and a fair way to test it: same thermometer, same shaded place, many readings.

items.p: A tumbler that is narrow at the bottom and wide at the top makes a good rain gauge.
items.why: False. Its wide top catches rain over a big opening, but the water collects in the narrow bottom, so it fills deeper than the true rain. A good rain gauge has straight sides, or a funnel of known size.

items.p: Divya's rain gauge shows 4 mm on Monday, 12 mm on Tuesday, 0 mm on Wednesday and 9 mm on Thursday. How much rain fell in the four days?
items.why: 4 + 12 + 0 + 9 = 25 mm. Adding the daily depths gives the total rainfall. A strong answer counts the 0 too, because a dry day is still a day in the record.

items.p: Revathi measured 10 mm of rain on her terrace in Madurai. The weather station 5 km away measured 25 mm. What is the most likely reason?
opts: One of the gauges must be broken
Rain does not fall evenly, so different places get different amounts
Rain gauges always give different numbers
items.why: A rain cloud can drop more rain in one place than another, even nearby. That is why IMD has many rain gauges, not one per city. A broken gauge is possible, but the first thing to think of is that the rain really was different.

items.p: Match each wind to where it comes from.
pairs: comes from the sea, to the east
comes from the southwest, over the Arabian Sea
items.why: Every wind is named for where it comes from. Chennai's sea lies to the east, so a breeze off the sea there comes from the east.

items.p: Why does a wind vane have a bigger tail than arrowhead? What would happen with a tiny tail?
items.a: The wind pushes harder on the bigger tail, so the tail swings away from the wind and the arrow ends up pointing into it. With a tiny tail and a big arrowhead, the arrowhead would be pushed away instead, and the vane would point the wrong way, or not settle.
items.why: A strong answer says that the wind pushes more on a bigger surface, and that is what turns the vane.

items.p: Sort these readings from a weather diary.
items.why: Degrees Celsius are temperatures, millimetres are rain, and a direction or a wind number describes the wind. A strong answer notices that 0 mm is still a rainfall reading.

items.p: Two sisters in Bengaluru look at the weather app. It says 30 °C, but 'feels like 34 °C'.

views.says: The real temperature is 30. A thermometer measured it. The 34 is just made up.
34 is more real. That's how hot it is for us. Who cares what a thermometer feels?

items.ask: Which sister do you agree with more? Explain. Then say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both are partly right. Anjali is right that 30 °C was measured in the shade, and that 'feels like' is worked out from a formula, not measured. Kavya is right that damp air and no wind make it feel hotter to people, and that matters for health. A good answer says each number answers a different question.
items.why: The measured temperature describes the air. The 'feels like' number tries to describe how people's bodies cope. Different apps work it out differently.

items.p: Why are weather screens painted white?
opts: White takes in little sunlight, so the box stays cool
White is easy to see from far away
items.why: A white surface reflects most sunlight. A dark box would heat up in the sun, warm the air inside, and the thermometer would read too high.

items.p: Draw a line chart for this day in Chennai: 7 am 27 °C, 10 am 31 °C, 1 pm 34 °C, 3 pm 35 °C, 6 pm 31 °C. Circle the warmest time.
items.a: A line rising from 27 to a peak of 35 at 3 pm, then falling to 31, with the 3 pm point circled.
items.why: A strong chart has the times evenly along the bottom, the temperatures up the side, and the highest point at 3 pm circled.
items.art: Empty axes labelled Time and Temperature (°C).

items.p: The highest temperature in a day is called the ____ temperature. The lowest is called the ____ temperature.
items.why: Maximum and minimum, often shortened to max and min in weather reports.

items.p: Three of these would make a thermometer read too high. Which one would not?
opts: Letting it touch a sunny wall
Hanging it in the shade with air all round
Putting it in a closed black box in the sun
items.why: In the shade with air round it, only the air warms it, so it reads correctly. The others all let sunlight or a hot surface heat it.

items.p: If the wind vane on your balcony keeps swinging about, your vane must be broken.
items.why: False. In a city, buildings and walls bend the wind and make it gusty, so a balcony vane often swings. A strong answer suggests watching for a minute and writing the direction it points most often.

items.p: Label this rain gauge: the funnel, the measuring jar, the ruler marks in mm, and the open sky above it.
items.why: The funnel leads rain into the jar. The marks show the depth in millimetres. The open sky above means nothing blocks or adds water. A strong answer says why each matters.
items.art: A rain gauge with a funnel on a jar standing on a terrace, with four empty label lines.

items.p: Anu has two thermometers. Before her test, she hangs them side by side in the shade. One reads 30 °C and the other 32 °C. What should she do before comparing sun and shade with them?
items.a: She should note that one reads 2 degrees higher than the other, and either correct for it, or use the same thermometer in both places. Otherwise a difference she sees might come from the thermometers, not from the sun.
items.why: A strong answer understands that tools must be checked against each other first, so the only difference in the test is the sunlight.

items.p: In Korea in 1441, people stopped measuring rain by digging into the soil. Why was the soil a poor rain gauge?
opts: Soil is too heavy to carry
Dry soil soaks up more rain than wet soil, so the same rain gave different answers
items.why: How deep the soil got wet depended on how dry it was before, and on the kind of soil. A metal vessel soaks up nothing, so it measures only the rain.

items.p: Here are three views about the thermometer at a bus stop in Hyderabad, which stands in the sun and shows 47 °C.

views.who: Zara, a girl waiting for the bus
views.says: It is 47 degrees. The sign says so.
The air is about 39. The sign is in the sun, so it is heating up.
Whatever the number, standing at this stop feels like 47.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use your Sun or Shade test as evidence. Then say what each of the others gets right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Usha about the air, using the Sun or Shade test: a thermometer in the sun reads many degrees above the shade. It also gives Zara her due: the sign really is at 47, which is true of the sign. It gives Gopal his due: a person standing in the sun is heated by sunlight too, just like the sign, so it can feel far hotter than the air.
items.why: Each view describes something true: the sign, the air, and a person standing in the sun. The weather report gives the air in the shade, because that can be fairly compared.

items.p: A family's flat terrace in Chennai is 40 square metres. 1 mm of rain on 1 square metre is 1 litre of water. How many litres fall on the terrace in a 5 mm shower?
items.why: 5 mm on 1 square metre is 5 litres. On 40 square metres it is 40 × 5 = 200 litres. A strong answer shows why rainwater harvesting from a terrace can collect a lot of water.

items.p: Meena makes a rain gauge from a straight jar 10 cm wide. Her friend makes one 5 cm wide. In the same rain, Meena's shows 8 mm. What will her friend's show?
items.why: Both have straight sides, so both fill to the same depth: 8 mm. Meena's catches four times as much water, because its opening is four times the area, but it spreads it over four times the floor.

items.p: Weather stations keep the thermometer about 1.25 to 2 metres above short grass, not on the ground. Why do you think the height matters?
items.a: The ground gets very hot in the day and cold at night. Air right next to it is much hotter or colder than the air we live in. Keeping the thermometer at the same height everywhere means readings can be compared.
items.why: A strong answer mentions that the ground heats and cools the air near it, and that a fixed height makes readings fair to compare.

items.p: The temperature in the weather report is the temperature on every street in the city.
items.why: False. It is the temperature at one weather station. Streets with many roads and few trees can be warmer, and parks can be cooler. A strong answer gives one reason a street might differ.

items.p: Design your own weather screen from things at home. Draw it, and label how it keeps sunlight out and lets air in.
items.a: Any design with a shade that stops all direct sunlight, gaps or slots for air, a light colour, and the thermometer hanging free inside.
items.why: A strong design gives a reason for each part, as the real weather screen does.
items.art: A blank space with a small sun drawn in one corner.

items.p: Put these in order, from the reading that is most likely to be too high to the one most likely to be right for the air.
items: A thermometer in a white slatted box in the shade
A thermometer lying on a black car roof in the sun
A thermometer hanging in full sun
A thermometer under a white paper roof in the sun
a: A thermometer lying on a black car roof in the sun
A thermometer hanging in full sun
A thermometer under a white paper roof in the sun
A thermometer in a white slatted box in the shade
items.why: The black roof heats the thermometer by touching it, on top of the sunlight. Full sun heats it directly. The paper roof shades it, but the paper warms a little. The weather screen is the best shade with air flowing through.

items.p: Your Sun or Shade test gave three different numbers on one balcony. Which number is 'the temperature'? Explain your answer.
items.a: Each number is true for the thermometer in that place. The temperature of the air is the shade reading, because there only the air was warming the thermometer. The sun reading was the thermometer's own temperature after sunlight heated it.
items.why: A strong answer says what each reading really measured, instead of just picking one.

items.p: A thermometer can only show how warm the ____ itself is.
items.why: A thermometer shows its own temperature. It shows the air's temperature only when the air is the only thing warming or cooling it.

items.p: Sort these as things weather stations do, or things they avoid.
items: read the tools at the same times every day
put the thermometer near a wall
use the same kind of rain gauge everywhere
keep the rain gauge under a tree
guess a reading that was missed
items.why: Weather stations follow the same rules everywhere and keep honest records. A missed reading is written as missed, never guessed, so the record can be trusted.

items.p: Label these four places on a drawing of a balcony: where the thermometer should hang, where the rain gauge should stand, where the wind vane should go, and one place to avoid.
a: thermometer in the shade, hanging free
rain gauge on the open edge under the sky
wind vane in the open, away from walls
avoid: the sunny wall or under the roof
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason for each place: shade for the thermometer, open sky for the rain gauge, open air for the vane.

items.p: Why do scientists keep weather records for many years in the same place, with the same tools?
opts: So they can tell real changes from one-off odd days
Because changing tools is too expensive
So the numbers always stay the same
items.why: One hot day says little. Many years of readings taken the same way show what is normal, and whether it is changing. If the tool or place changed, a difference might come from that and not from the weather.

open_questions.q: How much hotter will Indian cities get in the coming years?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists agree cities are warming, but the amount depends on how much the world warms and how cities are built, with or without trees and shade.

open_questions.q: Why does the monsoon reach Kerala on different dates each year?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on the oceans, the winds and the land all working together. Forecasts are getting better, but the exact date is still hard to predict.

open_questions.q: How can we measure rain fairly in strong wind?
open_questions.why_open: In strong wind, rain blows sideways and some misses the gauge, so gauges catch less than really fell. Scientists use shields and corrections, but no method is perfect.

open_questions.q: What is the best way to work out how hot weather 'feels' to a person?
open_questions.why_open: Different countries and apps use different formulas. Bodies differ too: a child, an old person and a labourer in the sun all feel the same weather differently.

maths.problem: In the Sun or Shade test, the thermometer read 44 °C in the sun and 33 °C in the shade. How many degrees higher was the sun reading?
maths.explain: 44 minus 33 is 11. Count on from 33: 34, 35 and so on up to 44 is 11 steps. So sunlight heated the thermometer 11 degrees above the air.
maths.context: This is about the Sun or Shade test, where one thermometer is hung in the sun, in the shade and under a paper roof.
maths.why_maths: Taking away one reading from another tells us exactly how much the sunlight added.

maths.problem: Under the paper roof the thermometer read 35 °C, and in the shade 33 °C. The challenge says a good weather screen must be within 2 degrees of the shade. Did the paper roof pass?
maths.answer: Yes, just. 35 minus 33 is 2 degrees, which is within 2 degrees.
maths.explain: 35 minus 33 is 2. The rule is 'within 2 degrees', so 2 is allowed. A reading of 36 would have failed, because 36 minus 33 is 3.
maths.context: This is about the Sun or Shade test and the Weather Screen challenge, where you try to keep sunlight off a thermometer.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the difference with a rule tells us whether a design is good enough, not just whether it is better.

maths.problem: Kavya's afternoon readings for one week were 34, 35, 33, 36, 35, 31 and 34 °C. On which day was it coolest, and what might explain it?
maths.answer: The sixth day, at 31 °C. It was probably a cloudy or rainy day.
maths.explain: 31 is the smallest number in the list. All the other days were 33 or more. A sudden drop like that often means clouds blocked the sunlight, so her sky drawing for that day is the place to check.
maths.context: This is about My Weather Diary, a 7-day project where you read a shade thermometer every afternoon.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart makes the odd day jump out, and then we ask what the weather did that day.

maths.problem: A family's flat terrace in Chennai is 30 square metres. One millimetre of rain on one square metre is one litre. How many litres fall on the terrace in a 10 mm shower?
maths.explain: 10 mm on one square metre is 10 litres. On 30 square metres it is 30 groups of 10 litres. 30 times 10 is 300 litres. That is about 15 big buckets.
maths.context: This is about measuring rain as a depth in millimetres, as in the Wide or Narrow test.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the depth by the area turns a rain gauge reading into real litres of water we could save.

maths.problem: In the day of readings, the thermometer read 28 °C at 7 am and 36 °C at 2 pm. How many hours passed, and how many degrees did it rise?
maths.explain: From 7 in the morning to 12 noon is 5 hours, and from noon to 2 pm is 2 more, so 7 hours. 36 minus 28 is 8 degrees. So the air warmed by a little over 1 degree each hour.
maths.context: This is about the day of readings, where you read a shade thermometer six times from morning to evening.
maths.why_maths: Working out the time and the rise together shows how quickly the air warms through the morning.

roots.context: We have measured the temperature, the rain and the wind. Now we ask what measuring tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the sun, your thermometer read many degrees higher than in the shade, in the same air. Sunlight was heating the thermometer itself. A thermometer can only show how warm it is. So to measure the air, we shade it, so that only the air can warm or cool it.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a measuring tool as a window that simply shows the world. But a thermometer is a thing in the world too. It takes part in what it measures, and its reading is what happened to it.
deep_truth.evidence: Under the white paper roof, in the same sunny spot, the reading fell back close to the shade reading. The air had not changed. Only the sunlight landing on the thermometer had changed.

three.who_am_i: Your skin is a kind of thermometer too. In a sunny patch it feels hot, even when the air is the same as in the shade.
three.what_is_life: Plants, birds and ants all sense the weather. A crow pants and sits in the shade on a hot afternoon, just as you would.
three.what_is_this_world: The same sunlight falls on the air, the ground and the walls. Each one takes in a different amount and warms in its own way.

roots.thread: On one balcony there is one Sun and one air. Yet your thermometer gave three numbers: one in the sun, one in the shade and one under paper. Each number was true. Each told what happened to the thermometer in that place. Each thing on the balcony meets the same sunlight and air in its own way. Many readings together, taken the same careful way, give a fuller picture than any one of them.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, in the Buddhist Pali Canon: the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: Several blind men each touched one part of an elephant. One felt the trunk, one the leg, one the ear. Each was sure the elephant was what he had touched.
teachings.link: Each thermometer reading was true for its own place, like each man's touch. Weather offices put many readings, taken the same way, together to see the whole.

teachings.teaching: The body is called the field. The one who knows the field is called the knower of the field.
teachings.link: A thermometer stands inside the field it measures. The sunlight on it is part of its reading, so we have to know where it stands to know what it is telling us.

science.text: A thermometer in direct sunlight can read far above the true air temperature. So the World Meteorological Organization asks for thermometers to be shaded and kept where air can flow round them.
In physics, every measurement involves the measuring tool meeting the thing measured. For everyday things like air, the tool's effect can be made very small, but not zero.

other_view.view: A thermometer in the sun is simply badly placed. Shade it properly, and it gives the air's temperature well enough for any weather use. There is no lesson about knowing here, only good and bad ways to set up a tool.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat, with the materials listed. Changes made: the Sun or Shade test needs a thermometer that reads up to at least 60 °C, because a fever thermometer reads only near body temperature and some wall thermometers stop at 50 °C. The thermometer hangs from a thread so that it touches nothing, because a sunny grill or ledge would heat it by touch. Each place gets 5 minutes and two readings a minute apart, which is enough for a glass or probe thermometer to settle. It needs a sunny spot and a shady spot close together, which most balconies or window grills have at some hour. On a cloudy day the difference is small, so the step says to try again on a sunny day. The Wide or Narrow test uses a bathroom shower, which every flat has, or a chalni and mugs of water, and it warns that tapered steel tumblers give a wrong depth. The rain gauge in the diary needs open sky, so the step says what to do if the balcony is fully roofed, and a dry week is treated as a real result. The wind vane swings in city gusts, so the step says to watch for a minute and note the usual direction. Both games work at home, and Be the Wind Vane needs only a phone compass and four paper signs. The spine fits about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: Nearly 600 years ago, in Korea, farmers needed rain for their rice, and the king's court kept records of the rain. To measure it, officials dug into the ground after the rain and looked at how deep the soil was wet. But this did not work well. Dry soil soaks up rain fast, while soil that is already wet takes in little more. Sandy soil and clay soil soak differently too. So the same rain gave different numbers in different places. The crown prince, who later became King Munjong, tried a better way. In 1441, he set a metal vessel in the palace courtyard and measured the depth of the rain in it with a ruler. A vessel soaks up nothing, so it shows only the rain. Soon after, the court sent rain gauges of the same size to towns all over the country. They were called cheugugi. Now the readings from different towns could be fairly compared. The wrong idea was that wet soil shows how much rain fell. The soil was also showing how dry it had been before.
how_we_found_out.who: Crown Prince Yi Hyang, who later became King Munjong, at the court of his father, King Sejong, in Joseon Korea
how_we_found_out.when: 1441, with rain gauges sent across the country soon after
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People measured rain by how deep it soaked into the soil. But the soil's own dryness, and the kind of soil, changed the answer. A metal vessel that soaks up nothing measured the rain alone.
